analysis.one_liner: Removes legal immunity for SPACs' rosy earnings projections, letting investors sue over hype.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 27-23 in November 2021, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the term ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: SPACs are shell companies that raise money from investors for the purpose of merging with a private company, which takes that company public without a traditional stock offering. Current federal law shields "blank check" companies from being sued over forward-looking statements — the growth and earnings projections used to pitch SPAC deals to investors. This bill would rewrite that shield so SPACs no longer qualify, meaning sponsors could be sued when their projections turn out to be false. The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee but never received a vote by the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors who buy SPAC shares. During the 2020-21 SPAC boom, retail investors poured money into these deals based largely on sponsor projections; many of the stocks collapsed after merging while sponsors collected large fees regardless. If this bill had passed, those investors would have had a legal remedy — the ability to sue sponsors and their banks over misleading forecasts — instead of bearing the loss alone.

how_it_helps.text: Strips SPACs of the legal shield from lawsuits over forward-looking statements. The bill amends both the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 so that a 'development stage company that has no specific business plan or purpose or has indicated that its business plan is to acquire or merge with an unidentified company' — the definition of a SPAC — is excluded from the safe harbor that normally protects such statements from liability.

Closes a loophole written for an earlier era. The existing law exempts 'blank check companies' from the safe harbor, but the modern SPAC boom exploited the gap between that old term and today's deal structures; the bill replaces the outdated phrase with language squarely covering SPACs.
Gives investors a way to hold sponsors accountable in court when a deal's projections prove false, instead of leaving them with only the sunk investment after a post-merger stock collapse.

analysis.who_pays: SPAC sponsors, the investment banks that underwrite SPAC deals, and companies going public through SPACs. Removing the safe harbor exposes them to investor lawsuits over projections, which would raise their legal risk, and likely make SPAC fundraising more expensive and cautious.
analysis.who_pays_short: SPAC sponsors and Wall Street underwriters

drawbacks.text: The shield exists for a reason: without it, SPACs might simply stop publishing projections altogether, so investors could end up with less information about a deal rather than more — and no basis to sue even when a deal sours.
Greater lawsuit exposure could make SPAC deals costlier and drive companies back to traditional IPOs, shrinking a cheaper and faster route to public markets that smaller firms have used.

The committee approved the bill only 'in the nature of a substitute (amended),' meaning the version that would have moved forward was substantially rewritten in committee; the final scope is not visible in the record, so investors could not know exactly what protections they were getting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real, documented harm: retail investors bought SPAC shares on sponsor forecasts that often collapsed after the merger, while sponsors collected their fees either way and faced no liability for the pitch. The costs — possible less disclosure, more litigation, and costlier deals — are genuine but are the same trade-offs securities law already imposes on ordinary public companies, which never had this shield. On balance, the bill offered a modest but real protection for investors at a cost concentrated on Wall Street dealmakers, though its value was blunted by dying before the House could vote on an amended version whose final terms were never made public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee in November 2021, but House leaders never brought it up for a floor vote, and it expired when the two-year term ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Del. Michael San Nicolas introduced the bill on November 9, 2021, with no cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
On November 16, 2021, the committee held a markup — a working session where members debate and amend a bill — and voted 27-23 to order it reported to the full House with a substitute amendment.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill was never reported to the floor and the full House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: SPAC sponsors and the banks that underwrite their deals are better off, because they kept the legal shield that protects their projections from investor lawsuits. Retail investors who bought into SPAC deals gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: SPAC sponsors and Wall Street underwriters

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 27-23, but the record does not show how those votes split by party, and with zero cosponsors there is no broader pattern to read.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the safe harbor that protects sponsors from being sued over the growth and earnings projections they use to sell SPAC shares. Sponsors earned large fees during the 2020-21 boom even when post-merger stocks collapsed, so liability for those pitches is a direct threat to their business model.

Banks underwrite SPAC offerings and would face greater exposure to fraud claims over deal projections if the safe harbor disappeared, raising the cost and risk of the SPAC business they profited from.

industries.industry: Private companies going public via SPAC
industries.note: These companies could no longer rely on shielded projections when merging with a SPAC, making the deals riskier and possibly costlier for them, though their investors would be better protected from hype.
